one_liner: LZMA2 encoder with a radix match finder: 1.3-1.6x faster than xz or the LZMA SDK at matching ratio, multithreaded, standard LZMA2 output.
what_it_does: A C library that produces LZMA2 streams (the codec inside .xz and .7z) faster than the reference encoder, plus a matching decoder. Its API is modeled on zstd's: one-shot FL2_compress/FL2_decompress (and Mt variants taking a thread count), reusable FL2_CCtx/FL2_DCtx contexts, a streaming FL2_CStream/FL2_DStream interface with timeouts and direct dictionary-buffer access, and FL2_CCtx_setParameter for fine-grained tuning. It is not API-compatible with liblzma; the companion FXZ Utils project wraps it behind a liblzma-derived interface and the .xz container, and it ships inside the 7-Zip-FL2, 7-Zip-zstd and p7zip forks.
how_it_is_fast: The core is a block-based radix match finder: it builds a match table for a whole dictionary-sized block by bucketing positions on their first one or two bytes and recursively lengthening and splitting the buffered chains up to a search depth, which parallelizes across threads without splitting the input into independent chunks or duplicating hash chains (extra memory per thread is a few MB, per the README). Higher levels add a hybrid mode with a small HC3 hash chain for short matches, and the encoder uses 7-Zip's optimal-parse LZMA2 encoder with some of Igor Pavlov's 18.05 improvements plus zstd-derived threading code. On x86-64 the Makefile also builds Igor Pavlov's assembler-optimized LZMA decoder (LZMA2_DEC_OPT), and multi-threaded decoding is possible because the encoder inserts dictionary resets every 4 dictionary sizes by default.
when_to_use: Building .xz/.7z-style archives, package payloads or backups at high LZMA2 levels where compression time dominates and decoders must stay standard LZMA2.
Multi-core compression of large single inputs: the radix match finder threads within one stream instead of splitting the file into independent chunks, so ratio holds up as thread count rises.
Replacing the LZMA SDK or liblzma encoder in a C or C++ tool that already handles raw LZMA2 or 7z containers (or through FXZ Utils when the .xz format and a liblzma-like API are needed).
Inputs of tens to hundreds of MB, where dictionaries of 16-128 MB and the higher levels (5-10) give the largest speed gain over the reference encoder.
when_not_to_use: Decode-bound workloads: decompression is no faster than LZMA SDK (lzbench 2.4: 78.5-79.1 MB/s vs lzma 26.03 at about 78 MB/s) and slower than xz 5.8.4's decoder in the same run (122-124 MB/s).
Low levels: at -1 the single-thread gain over xz -1 is small (21.8 vs 19.2 MB/s at 27.85% vs 27.75%); zstd or bzip3 cover the fast-but-strong range better.

Memory-constrained decoders: matching 7-Zip's ratio needs about twice the dictionary (README), and the lzbench rows that beat xz use large dictionaries (level 8: 64 MB, level 10: 128 MB per the level table in fl2_compress.c), which sets the decompressor's memory.
Projects that need an actively released library: the last tag is v1.0.1 (2019); development was idle from Aug 2020 to Oct 2025, and two later encoder memory-safety fixes exist only on master.
Callers expecting a drop-in .xz file writer from this repository alone: the native output is a raw LZMA2 stream with a property byte, not an .xz container.

integration.form: static lib / shared lib (GNU make builds both; VS2015 solution for a DLL)
integration.dependencies: none beyond pthreads (bundled xxhash, optional via NO_XXHASH)
integration.min_toolchain: C compiler with GNU make (gcc -O2 -pthread by default) or Visual Studio 2015; no CMake file in current releases
integration.platforms: portable C, 32- and 64-bit (32-bit dictionaries capped at 128 MB, 64-bit at 1 GB); x86-64 gets an optional assembler decoder
integration.thread_safety: not documented as such; state lives in per-call or caller-owned FL2_CCtx/FL2_DCtx/stream objects (zstd-style), and the library manages its own worker threads (up to 200)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — output is standard LZMA2 that liblzma's raw LZMA2 decoder and 7-Zip can read (FL2_p_omitProperties and FL2_getCCtxDictProp exist for 7-Zip/XZ embedding), but the API differs from liblzma and .xz containers need FXZ Utils

gotchas: Default levels use the same dictionary as 7-Zip and give output 1%-5% larger; FL2_p_highCompression selects a separate level table that compresses better on smaller dictionaries at a worse speed/ratio trade-off.
Multi-threaded decompression only works on streams that contain dictionary resets (FL2_p_resetInterval, default every 4 dictionary sizes); streams from xz or 7-Zip decode on one thread.

Out-of-bounds read in RMF_handleRepeat (issue #9, reported 2022, multi-threaded compression crash) was fixed only in January 2026 by PR #14, and an unsafe match-table access in LZMA2_ECtx_s was fixed in October 2025; neither is in a tagged release.

Build defaults differ by entry point: the root Makefile enables the x86-64 asm decoder, but embedders compiling the sources directly must define LZMA2_DEC_OPT and assemble lzma_dec_x86_64 themselves to get it.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Fast LZMA2 over xz/liblzma when you must emit standard LZMA2 for existing decoders and want the encode faster (1.5x at matched ratio single-threaded, more with threads); pick bzip3 or Kanzi instead when the format is free to change, since lzbench shows bzip3 -5 at 11.9 MB/s and a better ratio than any fastlzma2 level.
verified_claims_summary: lzbench 2.4 (gcc 15.2.0 release binary, one thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P with turbo off, silesia.tar) shows fastlzma2 1.0.1 -8 compressing at 4.52 MB/s to 23.18% vs xz 5.8.4 -7 at 3.01 MB/s to 23.15% (1.5x, derived from page data), and -10 at 3.38 MB/s to 22.96% vs lzma 26.03 -9 at 2.55 MB/s to 22.97% (1.3x, derived from page data); decompression in the same run is 79 MB/s vs xz's 122-124 MB/s. The README's 20%-100% gain over 7-Zip 19.00's LZMA2 encoder is a first-party two-thread chart with no numbers.
status_note: Dual BSD-3-Clause/GPL-2.0 and production-proven in several 7-Zip forks, but effectively in maintenance mode: v1.0.1 is from 2019, master gained two memory-safety fixes (2025-10, 2026-01), a CI workflow (2026-08) and a doc fix (2026-09-12), and issues asking whether the project is maintained (#13) or documented (#7) remain open.
